title: Faith and reason, 1870
hook: God can be known by reason from created things

segments.voice: Yesterday, infallibility, and how narrow it is. Your line was rarer than people think. The same council wrote a second document, and this one is about every thinking person, not just popes. Day seven hundred eighty-nine.

Why is there something rather than nothing? The philosopher Leibniz asked it that way, but children ask it without the polish, sometimes at bedtime. Why is there a world? Who made the first thing? A tired parent might say, go to sleep. The First Vatican Council, in a document called Dei Filius, decided the question deserved a straight answer about what a human mind can and cannot reach on its own. Today's word is Dei Filius, Vatican One's document on faith and reason.
screen: `WHY IS THERE ANYTHING?` → `A BEDTIME QUESTION.` → `FAITH AND REASON.`

segments.voice: The council made three claims, and they fit together. First, reason can reach God. Dei Filius teaches that God, the beginning and end of all things, can be known with certainty by the natural light of human reason, from the things he made. It takes that straight from Saint Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "For the invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made." You don't need a Bible to wonder where the world came from, and the council says the wondering can actually get somewhere. Second, reason is not the whole road. The same chapter says God also revealed himself, so that the truths about him that reason could reach might be known by everyone, easily, firmly and without error mixed in. And there are mysteries hidden in God, the council says, that reason could never find alone; Catholics name the Trinity as one. Third, the two cannot truly fight. In its fourth chapter the council says there can never be a real disagreement between faith and reason, because the same God who reveals the mysteries gave the mind its light. If they seem to clash, it says, either the faith has been misunderstood or an opinion has been mistaken for reason. Faith, it adds, should help reason, and reason should help faith. Notice what this council refused to do. It refused to say the mind is useless in religion, and it refused to say the mind is enough. That's today's line: reason reaches toward god.
screen: `REASON CAN REACH GOD.` · `REVELATION FILLS THE ROAD.` · `THEY CANNOT TRULY FIGHT.` · `NOT USELESS, NOT ENOUGH.` · then, large: `REASON REACHES TOWARD GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think about why there's anything at all. For the sit, pick one thing within reach: a cup, your own hand, the floor. Ask of it, slowly, why is this here, and then, why is there anything to be here at all? Don't hurry to an answer. Let the question stay open and see how far your mind goes with it. If you pray, you can let the question turn into thanks for the thing in front of you. The bell holds the time.
Dei Filius. The First Vatican Council's document teaching that faith and reason come from one God and can never truly contradict each other. Today's word.
Your line: reason reaches toward god. Today, when a hard question comes up, about God or anything else, give it a real thought instead of a shrug. Day seven hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching holds that God can be known by reason from the created world and also through revelation, and Catholic schools and universities teach philosophy alongside theology on that basis.

fork.setup: a child asks at bedtime why there's a world at all. by Dei Filius's lights, what's that question?
options: a silly question with no answer.
a real road the mind can travel toward God.
a question only scripture may answer.
fork.reveal: Vatican I taught that reason, starting from created things, can come to know God with certainty, while revelation shows more.

trapdoor: what you thought: faith and reason are opposites.
what it means: Vatican I taught that both come from one God, that reason can know him from creation, and that they cannot truly clash.
what a scholar hears: Dei Filius building on Romans 1:20, steering between trusting the mind for everything and trusting it for nothing.

notes: Romans 1:20 quoted from Douay-Rheims (Challoner); confirm exact punctuation, which differs slightly between printings.

Dei Filius ch. 2 (God knowable by natural reason; revelation so that all may know easily, with firm certainty and no error) and ch. 4 (no real disagreement; apparent conflicts come from misunderstood faith or opinions taken for reason; mutual help) are paraphrased. Confirm.
The Trinity is offered as an example of a mystery beyond reason; Dei Filius speaks of mysteries generally. Confirm this example is fine.
Leibniz's question ('why is there something rather than nothing') is attributed, paraphrased; confirm citation.
The year 1870 appears only in the index title.
Editor: softened 'usually at bedtime' and 'parents tend to say' (uncited generalizations); the Trinity is now offered as the Catholic example rather than as the council's own words.
